output.title: Rising claims-interpretation ticket cluster: readiness score misread as clinical result
output.summary: Feedback tagged claims-interpretation rose sharply between the prior and current windows (see {f_2} and {f_1}), spread across five firmware versions, three app versions, and five regions, with no concentration on any single build. Sampled tickets describe wearers treating the readiness score as a diagnostic or clinical result (cancelling a meeting, showing a screenshot to a partner as a clinical finding), matching the claims-misread queue described in the support playbook (KD-03) and the wellness-claims policy (KD-05). This pattern closely matches a previously closed incident, INC-2025-002, which was confirmed as a communications/copy risk rather than a device or sensor defect. The lack of firmware/app-version concentration and the qualitative match to that precedent support the same read here: this is a real regulatory/communications risk driven by on-screen copy or messaging, not a hardware or sensor malfunction.

leading_hypothesis.statement: The rise in claims-interpretation tickets reflects wearers misreading the readiness score as a clinical/diagnostic result, an association with on-screen copy/UX rather than a firmware or sensor defect, consistent with the previously closed communications incident INC-2025-002.

alternative_hypotheses.statement: A specific firmware or app release introduced a change in the score's presentation that triggered the misread cluster.
alternative_hypotheses.falsifying_test: Breakdown of claims-interpretation ticket counts by firmware_version and app_version showed spread across versions 1.2.0 through 1.4.2 and app 3.0 through 3.2, with no single version dominating, weakening a version-specific UI regression story.

alternative_hypotheses.statement: This is a device/sensor accuracy defect (data-accuracy) rather than a comms/claims issue, since many tickets carry both tags together.
alternative_hypotheses.falsifying_test: Would need a telemetry comparison (e.g. motion_intensity or skin_temp_delta_c anomalies) tied to the same device IDs in the sampled tickets to rule in/out an actual sensor-accuracy fault underlying the perceived misread.

supporting_evidence.claim: Sampled current-window tickets show wearers describing the readiness score as a health verdict, lab result, or clinical finding, and acting on it (cancelling a meeting, showing a partner).
Sampled tickets span firmware versions 1.2.0 through 1.4.2 and app versions 3.0 through 3.2 and multiple regions, indicating no single build or region is driving the cluster.

The support playbook defines a distinct claims-misread intake queue tagged claims-interpretation (often alongside data-accuracy) whose remediation is a factual, non-medical restatement of the score's purpose, not a device fix.

A prior incident with a similarly claims-shaped ticket cluster was confirmed as a communications incident, not a device incident, and closed via copy review and a policy update rather than a scoring-code rollback.
Company policy explicitly separates hardware/radio telemetry from wellness/clinical claims, underscoring that a claims-misread cluster is a messaging risk category distinct from a sensor defect.

counter_evidence.claim: Prior-window sample tickets show some users correctly self-correcting after reading help content, suggesting the underlying copy/help material is not universally confusing.

recommended_actions.description: Escalate the claims-interpretation ticket cluster to Communications/Regulatory for copy review of the readiness score presentation, per KD-05 policy, given the sharp rise in ticket volume.
Have support staff apply the KD-03 claims-misread script (factual, non-medical restatement of score purpose) on open and incoming tickets in this queue.

If copy review confirms on-screen text is the proximate trigger, file a copy bug and consider an in-app clarification of the wellness-only nature of the score before any external communication is issued.

uncertainty: It is not yet confirmed which specific UI copy or app screen is driving the misread; only the ticket-cluster pattern and its resemblance to a prior closed comms incident are established.
Overlap with data-accuracy tags in most sampled tickets leaves open whether a subset of cases also involves an actual sensor/scoring accuracy issue rather than pure misinterpretation.
Sample size for qualitative review was small relative to the full current and prior ticket counts; broader manual ticket review would strengthen the comms-vs-defect distinction.

output.title: Overheating tag cluster in Nordics resolves to known cold-weather battery/UI pattern, not a thermal event
output.summary: Leading hypothesis holds that overheating tags are a byproduct of Nordics cold-weather battery drain and an alarming sync-screen UI rather than real thermal events. The falsifying test is: find overheating-tagged feedback describing genuine device heat/burn that is not co-tagged with battery or app-ui, in any region. This search returned zero matching records in the current window, and skin_temp_delta_c is flat and near-uniform across all regions, so the falsification attempt did not succeed this pass; status remains as given pending broader sampling.

leading_hypothesis.statement: The overheating-tagged tickets are a byproduct of a known Nordics cold-weather battery-drain characteristic and an alarming sync-screen UI, co-reported with the overheating tag, rather than evidence of an actual thermal/safety event; this is a correlational reading of the feedback co-tagging pattern, not a mechanism claim.

alternative_hypotheses.statement: A genuine subset of overheating-tagged tickets reflects real device heat/thermal discomfort (independent of the cold-weather battery-drain/UI narrative), which could be masked by aggregate co-tagging with battery and app-ui tags.
alternative_hypotheses.falsifying_test: Search overheating-tagged feedback for records describing device heat/burn on skin that are NOT co-tagged with battery or app-ui, across any region, in the current window; a non-trivial count of such standalone thermal-complaint records would falsify the leading hypothesis that all overheating tags trace to cold-weather battery drain and sync-screen UI. A direct search for this pattern returned {f_6} matching records.

deterministic_findings.label: Feedback records matching overheating tag, current window
Feedback records matching overheating tag, prior window
skin_temp_delta_c rate, current window, Nordics region only

supporting_evidence.claim: All sampled overheating-tagged feedback records in both windows are region nordics and co-tagged with battery and app-ui, describing cold-weather drain and a warm/alarming sync screen rather than a hot device on skin.
The overheating-tagged ticket volume ({f_3} current versus {f_4} prior) is essentially flat between windows, consistent with the candidate's own falling-trend flag rather than an emerging cluster.
skin_temp_delta_c fell slightly from the prior window ({f_2}) to the current window ({f_1}) at the fleet level, the opposite direction from what a true escalating thermal event would show.

Knowledge base explicitly documents that skin_temp_delta_c has near-zero correlation with battery_drain_pct on Nordics device-days and warns against using it to validate a cold-weather or overheating narrative; it also documents a prior closed incident with the same Nordics winter-drain-ticket shape, closed as not-an-incident and encoded as a standing known issue.

counter_evidence.claim: Nordics current-window skin_temp_delta_c ({f_5}) is nominally higher than the comparison UK figure cited in the known-issues register, though the knowledge base states this magnitude is not diagnostic of true ambient or core heat and sits well within the field's normal range.

A targeted search for overheating-tagged feedback describing a device hot-to-touch or burn/thermal experience returned zero matching records in the current window, and skin_temp_delta_c is essentially flat and near-identical across all five regions (benelux, dach, iberia, nordics, uk) rather than elevated specifically in Nordics or in any region, which is consistent with (not falsifying of) the leading hypothesis but is the required check for falsification.
